scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: In snowy cities, trucks spread salt on icy roads, and the ice melts even below zero. How?

scenes.name: balance
scenes.text: At zero degrees, water molecules are constantly freezing onto ice, and melting off it, at the same rate.

scenes.name: dissolve
scenes.text: Salt dissolves in the thin layer of water on the ice, splitting into sodium and chloride ions.

scenes.name: block
scenes.text: Those ions get in the way, so fewer water molecules freeze back on. Melting wins.

scenes.name: point
scenes.text: This lowers the freezing point. Salty water stays liquid at temperatures where pure water would freeze.

scenes.name: limit
scenes.text: It has limits. Below about minus ten degrees, common salt works poorly, so other chemicals are used.

scenes.name: kulfi
scenes.text: The same trick makes ice cream. Ice plus salt gets colder than plain ice, freezing the cream faster.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Dissolve, block, lower the freezing point. Follow for more on how things really work.
